new_statements.rule_in_words: In routine (non-emphatic) speech, word stress falls on the penultimate syllable: disyllables are stressed on the first syllable, trisyllables on the second; stress is predictable. Under emphasis, or when an object noun conveys new information, stress moves to the final syllable ('stress sandhi'); the syllable carrying sentence stress gets extra-high pitch. Corroborated second-hand for the Colombian (Caimán Nuevo) variety by Llerena 1986: 48 ('en la palabra aislada recae, con muy pocas excepciones, en la penúltima sílaba. Los sintagmas dañan esta tendencia').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the recovered snippets (for San Blas Kuna, Smith 2014: 49 reports secondary stress on the penult of words longer than four syllables).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifts to the final syllable when a word is emphasized and on an object noun that provides new information; 'stress may occur on the first syllable of a three-syllable word, especially in words which, [..]' (condition cut off in the snippet); Llerena adds 'con muy pocas excepciones' and that phrases (sintagmas) disturb the penultimate tendency.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, 'routine speech' (citation/normal register); the article is centrally about stress sandhi at phrase/sentence level (emphatic and information-structure shifts, extra-high pitch on sentence stress). Paya dialect, Darién, Panama, 600-800 speakers per the article.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes the Paya dialect (villages of Paya and Púcuro, Darién, Panama; 600-800 speakers), which is the Panamanian side of Border Kuna [kvn] = bord1248. Llerena's corroborating statement is for the Kuna of Caimán Nuevo (Antioquia, Colombia), also kvn. Smith 2014 and Holmer 1947 (held by the project, also penultimate/weight-based) describe San Blas Kuna (sanb1242), not this language.

sources.note: 'As a general rule, the penultimate syllable of a Kuna word is stressed (Smith 2014: 48-9). In stressed open syllables, vowels are automatically long (Llerena Villalobos 2000: 66; Adelaar & Muysken 2004: 62)'; 'There is neither tone nor distinctive vowel nasality in Kuna.' Secondary synthesis of Kuna in general.

sources.note: San Blas/Gardi Guna (sanb1242), not Border Kuna: 'In roots, the stress always falls on the penultimate (second to last) syllable'; clitics do not affect main stress; secondary stress on the penult in words longer than four syllables. p. 25 notes Forster 1977 proposed 'Border Guna' as a separate language.

sources.note: San Blas Cuna (consultant Pérez Kantule): 'the Cuna stress system.. depends altogether on the nature of the syllables.. no free accentuation.. The accent thus bears evenly on all long vowels or short vowels followed by a double or geminated consonant.. final closed syllables are never marked with an accent' (p. 23). No Paya/Colombian data.
